Your Daily AI Press Review — May 29, 2026: Funding Surge.

Anthropic closes a $65 billion Series H at a $965 billion valuation, overtaking OpenAI and reporting $47 billion in annualized revenue — the biggest private AI funding round in history. Cognition, maker of coding agent Devin, more than doubles its valuation to $26 billion in under nine months. Snowflake commits $6 billion to AWS in a multiyear infrastructure deal. Off the radar, a Tajik-language foundation model built on Gemma 3 is running an education-sector pilot across Central Asia — a signal the mainstream has missed entirely.

Anthropic raised $65 billion in a Series H round, pushing its post-money valuation to $965 billion and overtaking OpenAI, which was last valued at $730 billion. The round was led by Altimeter Capital, Dragoneer, Greenoaks, and Sequoia Capital, with each lead investor contributing more than $2 billion. The $65 billion includes $15 billion in previously committed hyperscaler investments, of which Amazon contributed $5 billion. Micron Technology, which recently crossed a $1 trillion market cap, also participated. Anthropic said its annualized run-rate revenue crossed $47 billion earlier this month, up from $30 billion in April and $14 billion at the start of the year.

Alongside the Series H, Anthropic shipped its latest flagship model, Claude Opus 4.8, which the company describes as a modest but tangible improvement over its predecessor. The new model outperforms OpenAI's latest and Google's Gemini 3.1 Pro on most benchmarks and catches its own coding errors four times more often than the prior generation. Anthropic is simultaneously rolling out dynamic workflows capable of spinning up hundreds of parallel sub-agents to handle tasks such as codebase-wide migrations. The llm-anthropic open-source plugin was updated the same day to expose the new model and a fast-mode option for enterprise accounts.

Cognition, the company behind AI software developer Devin, raised over $1 billion at a valuation above $26 billion — more than double its valuation from nine months ago. The round is one of the clearest signals of how much investor capital is flowing into AI coding agents, even as their real-world productivity gains remain actively debated. Cognition has not disclosed the round's lead investors or its current revenue. The valuation jump from roughly $10 billion to $26 billion in under a year places Cognition among the fastest-appreciating private AI companies in the current cycle.

Snowflake committed $6 billion to AWS in a multiyear strategic collaboration agreement aimed at accelerating enterprise agentic AI adoption. The deal covers joint infrastructure for building and deploying AI across Snowflake's global customer base. Snowflake did not break out the annual spend cadence, but the total commitment is one of the largest cloud infrastructure pledges from a data platform company. The agreement deepens an existing relationship between the two companies and positions Snowflake's data cloud as a primary substrate for agentic workloads running on AWS compute.

Alibaba's Qwen3.7-Max model scored 1,541 on the Code Arena ranking, claiming the fourth spot globally and making Alibaba the only developer other than Anthropic to break into the top five. The other four top-five positions are held by various Claude iterations. Separately, Alibaba launched MuleRun, an agent platform showcased at the Alibaba Cloud summit on May 20, billed as an always-on AI workforce offering one-stop access to a range of specialized agents. Alibaba also confirmed that Qwen3.7-Max includes tool-calling capabilities designed to act as a digital brain for robotics, triggering physical navigation and hardware actions.

Mistral AI rebranded its Le Chat chatbot as Vibe and bundled chat, coding agents, and a new Work Mode under one product. Work Mode integrates directly with Google Workspace, Outlook, Slack, and GitHub, handling emails, reports, and pull requests autonomously. The rebrand positions Mistral more directly against agent-based offerings from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. Separately, Airbus announced a partnership with Mistral AI to deploy AI in sovereign aerospace applications, making Mistral one of the few European AI labs to land a major defense-adjacent industrial contract.

Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.5 reached third place on Arena's text-to-image leaderboard, pulling even with Google's Nano Banana 2 but still trailing OpenAI's Image-2. The model shows clear gains over its predecessor, particularly in rendering text inside images and generating commercial visuals. Microsoft also launched a redesigned version of Microsoft 365 Copilot that the company claims loads twice as fast, with more structured and scannable responses rolling out across desktop and mobile. The two releases mark Microsoft's most visible consumer-facing AI product updates in several weeks.

Goldman Sachs published a report finding that agentic AI workloads may increase token demand by as much as 24 times compared with standard LLM usage. Uber and Microsoft are cited among companies already feeling the cost pressure of tokenized billing as agent usage scales. The report frames cost-per-token and performance-per-watt as the two metrics that will define enterprise AI economics in the agentic era. NVIDIA's own blog on AI factories published the same week echoes the framing, describing data centers as token factories where power-to-intelligence conversion efficiency is the primary competitive variable.

Tencent Cloud launched WorkBuddy, a productivity-focused AI agent for global users after an initial China rollout. WorkBuddy accepts natural language prompts to break down tasks, call external tools, and generate deliverables across office and study workflows. It supports remote task execution, positioning it as a direct competitor to Microsoft 365 Copilot and Google Workspace's Duet AI in enterprise productivity. Tencent's move into the global agent market follows Alibaba's MuleRun launch and signals that Chinese cloud platforms are now actively competing for enterprise agent budgets outside their home market.

On deployments. Verizon Connect built an agentic AI solution on AWS and scaled it to 100,000 daily users, converting overwhelming fleet telematics data into clear, actionable operational insights. The company used Amazon Bedrock's agent infrastructure and a two-layer architecture separating batch processing from real-time interaction. Verizon Connect has not disclosed specific latency or cost figures publicly, but the AWS case study describes measurable reductions in the time fleet managers spend interpreting raw data. At 100,000 daily users, it's one of the largest disclosed agentic AI deployments in the logistics and fleet management sector.

AWS's own Sales, Marketing and Global Services division deployed NarrateAI, a conversational business intelligence assistant built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The system uses specialized AI agents for intelligent routing and validation, separating batch analytics from real-time query handling. AWS describes it as delivering business intelligence at scale for an organization that spans thousands of account teams globally. The deployment is notable because it's an internal AWS use case — the company is running its own agentic architecture on the same infrastructure it sells to enterprise customers.

Penn Medicine and K Health announced a partnership to deploy AI clinical agents across Penn's health system. The collaboration targets clinical decision support and patient-facing workflows, with K Health contributing its AI clinical reasoning layer and Penn Medicine providing the care delivery infrastructure. Neither party disclosed the number of patients or clinicians in scope at launch, but Penn Medicine serves roughly 40,000 employees and millions of patients annually across its Philadelphia-area network. The deal is one of the first major academic medical center deployments of an externally developed AI clinical agent platform.

Payroll startup Remote surpassed $300 million in annual recurring revenue and reached cash-flow positive status, attributing a 50 percent increase in revenue per employee directly to AI adoption — without adding headcount. The company did not specify which AI tools drove the gain, but the result is one of the clearest published data points on AI's impact on per-employee productivity in a software business. Remote operates across more than 180 countries, making the efficiency gain significant at scale. The cash-flow positive milestone arrived roughly two years after the company's last major funding round.

Citigroup's Hong Kong office began piloting Arc, an in-house AI agent platform initially targeting software developers and engineers. The rollout is notable because it uses US-built AI technology in a market where geopolitical tensions are creating pressure on American software access. Arc is described as capable of handling developer workflows autonomously. Citi has not disclosed the number of engineers in the pilot or the underlying model provider. Several other leading American banks are running similar AI tool deployments in Hong Kong, according to the South China Morning Post, despite the regulatory uncertainty.

Indian ride-hailing platform Rapido disclosed that over 60 percent of its coding is now done by AI, according to cofounder Rishikesh SR. The company did not specify which AI coding tools it uses or the size of its engineering team, but the figure places Rapido among the most aggressive disclosed adopters of AI-assisted development in South and Southeast Asia. Separately, Indian payroll and HR platform data shows AI-native startups across Southeast Asia are building leaner teams and embedding agents into daily workflows, with hiring increasingly concentrated in roles AI cannot yet perform.

Amazon MGM Studios and AWS launched a GenAI Creators' Fund that gives filmmakers funding and access to an in-house AI production platform called Project Nara. Three animated series are already in production for Prime Video, with pilot teams given five weeks to complete their episodes. Amazon describes Project Nara as the only end-to-end AI content ecosystem in the industry. The move puts Amazon in direct competition with traditional animation studios and signals that AI-generated long-form video content is moving from proof-of-concept to scheduled broadcast programming.

On tools. NVIDIA released Polar, a rollout framework that lets researchers run reinforcement learning over any existing agent harness — Codex, Claude Code, Qwen Code, or others — without modifying the harness itself. Polar places a model API proxy between the harness and the inference server, capturing token-level interactions and reconstructing trainer-ready trajectories. Using GRPO on a Qwen3.5-4B base model, Polar improved SWE-Bench Verified pass@1 by 22.6 points under the Codex harness, 4.8 points under Claude Code, and 6.2 points under Pi. The framework is registered as a NeMo Gym environment and released under the ProRL Agent Server repository.

The TokenSpeed inference engine set a new GPU throughput record of 580 tokens per second running Alibaba's largest mixture-of-experts model on standard GPU hardware. The gain comes from systematic elimination of memory copies during inference, a technique applicable to other large sparse models. For teams running agentic workloads where multiple model calls chain together, a near-600-token-per-second throughput floor materially changes the economics of multi-step reasoning pipelines. The benchmark was published on the PyTorch blog and is reproducible on current-generation GPU clusters without specialized hardware modifications.

Perplexity AI open-sourced a rewritten Unigram tokenizer that achieves five times lower median latency than the Hugging Face tokenizers library and cuts production CPU utilization by five to six times. The tool is a drop-in replacement for teams using Unigram-based tokenization in reranking pipelines. At scale, a five-to-six times CPU reduction translates directly to infrastructure cost savings for any team running high-throughput retrieval-augmented generation. Perplexity released the code publicly without restrictions, making it immediately available to any engineering team running Rust-based inference infrastructure.

Liquid AI released LFM2.5-8B-A1B, an on-device mixture-of-experts model with 8.3 billion total parameters but only 1.5 billion active at inference time. The model supports a 128,000-token context window, reasoning, and tool calling on consumer hardware. For enterprise teams evaluating on-premise or edge deployments — where data sovereignty or latency requirements rule out cloud APIs — a model with this capability profile running on a single consumer GPU represents a meaningful new option. Liquid AI has not disclosed benchmark comparisons against similarly sized dense models, but the active-parameter efficiency is the key design claim.

Google Pay introduced the Universal Commerce Protocol, a new server architecture designed to handle purchases executed by AI agents rather than human users. The update positions Google Pay as a clearinghouse for agent-initiated transactions — bookings, subscriptions, procurement — where no human is present at checkout. The protocol is live and available to developers building agent workflows that require payment execution. For enterprise architects designing agentic systems that touch procurement or expense management, Google Pay's Universal Commerce Protocol is now a concrete integration option rather than a roadmap item.

One signal to watch. Token cost is becoming a board-level number. Goldman Sachs estimates agentic workloads could multiply token demand by 24 times, and Microsoft's internal experience with Claude Code — deployed to thousands of developers before being pulled back due to cost — confirms the dynamic is already live in production. Gartner separately warned that most generative AI and custom model projects will fail, with adoption friction and cost overruns as the primary culprits. The combination of Goldman's 24-times multiplier and Microsoft's cost reversal suggests enterprises are entering a second phase of AI budgeting where token economics, not seat licenses, drive the conversation.

Chinese AI companies are moving faster than Western coverage suggests on two fronts simultaneously. Kuaishou's Kling AI video generator posted revenue growth of over 300 percent in a single quarter, reaching 650 million yuan on a base of 33.7 billion yuan in total company revenue. MiniMax hit 1 million enterprise and developer clients, up fivefold in six months from roughly 200,000. Both companies are profitable-path businesses, not pure research labs. Alibaba's pivot to embodied AI for robotics — with Qwen3.7-Max providing tool-calling for physical hardware — adds a third vector. The pattern across Kuaishou, MiniMax, and Alibaba is commercialization at speed, not benchmark competition.

Memory and storage are emerging as the binding constraint on AI infrastructure scaling. SK Hynix crossed a $1 trillion market capitalization on AI chip demand, joining Micron — which also crossed $1 trillion and participated in Anthropic's Series H — in the trillion-dollar club. China's CXMT cleared its Shanghai Stock Exchange IPO review the same week, and YMTC entered its IPO guidance period on May 19. The International Semiconductor Industry Association projects global memory output will exceed $550 billion in 2026. Industry analysts quoted in Chinese state media describe storage as a permanent bottleneck: AI is short on chips in the near term, short on energy in the medium term, and short on storage indefinitely.

Off the radar. Researchers in Tajikistan built Soro, a family of Tajik-language LLMs starting from open-weight Gemma 3 checkpoints, trained on a 1.9-billion-token corpus of filtered web text, PDFs, and curriculum-aligned educational materials, then fine-tuned on 40,000 teacher-style examples. Soro substantially outperforms same-size Gemma 3 baselines on Tajik benchmarks while retaining strong English performance. FP8 and INT4 quantization preserves most of the Tajik-language gains while reducing memory requirements for edge deployment. An education-sector pilot is already running, with a planned scale-out across schools — a low-resource language AI deployment that has received no coverage in Western tech media.

Azercell Telecom, Azerbaijan's largest mobile operator, trained an Azerbaijani-language LLM on Amazon SageMaker AI in a six-week collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. The challenge was adapting foundation models to a morphologically rich language with limited training data and no existing blueprint for efficient LLM training in Azerbaijani. The result is a production-ready framework for a telecom use case and a customer-facing chatbot. Together with Soro in Tajikistan, the Azercell project signals that Central Asian telecoms are building sovereign language AI infrastructure — a market segment that Western AI labs have not prioritized.

iFlytek unveiled AI smart glasses weighing 40 grams at BEYOND Expo 2026 in Macau, featuring the GlassClaw AI agent and advanced noise recognition. The device is designed for real-world ambient AI interaction, not screen-based interfaces. XREAL's CEO, speaking at the same event, predicted an iPhone-equivalent inflection point for AI glasses within two years. Chinese hardware companies including iFlytek, XREAL, and Om AI Technology are converging on edge AI devices as the next deployment surface — a hardware race that is largely invisible in US and European AI coverage but represents a significant volume market given China's consumer electronics manufacturing scale.

Foxconn is beginning to ship next-generation optical interconnect technology for AI data centers, according to Nikkei Asia. The shift from copper to optical interconnects inside data centers reduces latency and power consumption at the rack level — a constraint that becomes critical as token throughput targets rise toward the 580-tokens-per-second range now achievable on GPU clusters. Foxconn's entry into optical data center components, alongside its existing server assembly business, positions the company as a vertically integrated AI infrastructure supplier. This is a supply-chain development with direct implications for hyperscaler build-out timelines that has not surfaced in mainstream AI coverage.

On the research front. Alibaba Research published GUI-RobustEval and the RoTS framework, addressing a critical gap in GUI agent deployment: the inability to recover from self-induced errors. RoTS synthesizes 800,000 high-quality training trajectories using a tree-based pipeline that proactively discovers error modes and generates recovery steps. The resulting RoTS-32B model achieves a 47.4 percent success rate on OSWorld — the most demanding GUI agent benchmark — with a 33.8 percent All-Pass@4 score. For enterprise teams deploying agents on desktop or web interfaces, error recovery capability is the primary barrier to unattended operation, and this result moves that bar measurably.

Researchers introduced COLAGUARD, a safety guardrail model that transfers multi-step reasoning into a continuous latent space rather than generating explicit text rationales. Evaluated across ten moderation settings spanning eight safety benchmarks, COLAGUARD improves macro-F1 by 8.24 points over Llama Guard 3 while delivering a nearly 13 times speedup and a 22 times reduction in token usage compared to an explicit reasoning baseline. For production deployments where safety checks run on every inference call, a 13-times latency improvement at equivalent accuracy is a direct infrastructure cost reduction. The result suggests latent reasoning is a viable path to deployable guardrails at scale.

CLUBench, a new clustering benchmark from academic researchers, evaluated 24 algorithms across 131 datasets in nearly 180,000 experiments covering tabular, text, and image data. The headline finding: deep clustering methods show no significant advantage over the best conventional algorithms when hyperparameters are properly tuned. Foundation model-based clustering performs well on text but does not generalize cleanly to tabular data. For data teams evaluating whether to adopt deep learning-based clustering in financial or operational datasets, the benchmark provides the first large-scale empirical basis for that decision — and the answer is that classical methods remain competitive when tuned correctly.

Researchers published ORACLE-SWE, a framework that isolates and quantifies the contribution of individual information signals — reproduction tests, regression tests, edit location, execution context, and API usage — to software engineering agent performance on SWE-Bench. The key finding is that providing oracle-quality edit location information alone produces the largest single performance gain among all tested signals, larger than execution context or test availability. For teams building or procuring AI coding agents, the result identifies where to invest in tooling: precise file and function localization before the agent begins editing produces more reliable outcomes than richer runtime feedback.
